'''David S. Goodsell''' is an American scientific illustrator and biologist who is an associate professor at the [[Scripps Research Institute]]<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://vivo.scripps.edu/display/GoodsellDavid|title=CV of Goodsell, David|website=vivo.scripps.edu|language=en|access-date=2019-07-11|archive-date=2020-09-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200929144913/https://vivo.scripps.edu/display/GoodsellDavid|url-status=dead}}</ref> and research professor at [[Rutgers, New Jersey|Rutgers University, New Jersey]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchwithrutgers.com/en/persons/david-goodsell|title=Profile: David Goodsell|website=researchwithrutgers.com|publisher=Rutgers University|access-date=2019-07-13}}</ref> (dual appointment). Goodsell is especially well known for his watercolor paintings of cell interiors, and for the creation of an enormous repertoire of educational resources as the founder of [[Protein Data Bank|RSCB Protein Data Bank's]] [[Molecule of the Month]].<ref name="cohen-science">{{cite journal |last1=Cohen |first1=Jon |title=Meet the scientist painter who turns deadly viruses into beautiful works of art |journal=Science |date=11 April 2019 |doi=10.1126/science.aax6641|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="goodsell-gallery">{{cite web |title=PDB101: Goodsell Gallery |url=https://pdb101.rcsb.org/sci-art/goodsell-gallery |website=RCSB: PDB-101 |access-date=5 May 2021}}</ref>

== Career and research ==
Goodsell obtained a Bachelor's of Science in both biology and chemistry from the [[University of California, Irvine|University of California Irvine]] in 1982.<ref name=":2" /> After this, he completed a PhD in X-ray crystallography of DNA at the [[University of California, Los Angeles|University of California Los Angeles]] in 1987.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Taylor |first=Michelle |date=2019-06-17 |title=The Intersection of Art and Science |url=https://www.laboratoryequipment.com/article/2019/06/intersection-art-and-science |url-status= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190618022455/https://www.laboratoryequipment.com/article/2019/06/intersection-art-and-science |archive-date=June 18, 2019 |access-date=2019-07-11 |website=Laboratory Equipment |language=en}}</ref> Since completing his PhD he has worked as a [[Structural biology|structural biologist]] at the [[Scripps Research Institute]] (with a 2-year period in [[University of California, Los Angeles|University of California]] in 1992–94).<ref name=":2" /> 

His research topics have included the use of structural biology and [[Molecular dynamics|molecular dynamic simulations]] to investigate symmetry in protein oligomers, [[Protein–protein interaction|protein–protein interactions]] and for [[computer-aided drug design]]. In particular he is a developer of [[AutoDock]], the most widely used program used for [[Docking (molecular)|molecular docking]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sousa|first1=Sérgio Filipe|last2=Fernandes|first2=Pedro Alexandrino|last3=Ramos|first3=Maria João|date=2006|title=Protein–ligand docking: Current status and future challenges|journal=Proteins: Structure, Function, and Bioinformatics|language=en|volume=65|issue=1|pages=15–26|doi=10.1002/prot.21082|pmid=16862531|s2cid=21569704|issn=1097-0134}}</ref> His main research focus areas are [[HIV drug resistance]] and structure and function of [[Bacterial cell structure|bacterial cells]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ccsb.scripps.edu/goodsell/science/|title=Goodsell Home Page: Science|last=Goodsell|first=David|website=scripps.edu|access-date=2019-07-20}}</ref>

Goodsell's illustrations are frequently used as teaching tools,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Goodsell|first1=David S.|last2=Franzen|first2=Margaret A.|last3=Herman|first3=Tim|date=2018-10-19|title=From Atoms to Cells: Using Mesoscale Landscapes to Construct Visual Narratives|journal=Journal of Molecular Biology|volume=430|issue=21|pages=3954–3968|doi=10.1016/j.jmb.2018.06.009|pmid=29885327|pmc=6186495|issn=0022-2836}}</ref> in textbooks, in scientific publications,<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/meet-scientist-painter-who-turns-deadly-viruses-beautiful-works-art |title=Meet the scientist painter who turns deadly viruses into beautiful works of art |last=Cohen |first=Jon |date=2019-04-11 |website=Science}}</ref> and as journal cover art.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Söderqvist|first=Thomas|date=2010|title=Selling point: David Goodsell|journal=Nature Medicine|language=en|volume=16|issue=9|pages=943|doi=10.1038/nm0910-943|pmid=20823862|s2cid=2731570|issn=1078-8956|doi-access=free}}</ref> In graduate school, Goodsell became interested in [[scientific illustration]] while writing molecular graphics programs to visualize protein and [[DNA]] structures. His images of individual proteins are typically computer generated, [[Cel shading|cell-shaded]] space-filling representations of proteins, often with cut-aways to show internal [[Binding site|binding sites]] and [[Cofactor (biochemistry)|cofactors]]. 

By contrast, Goodsell's [[Watercolor painting|watercolor]] paintings of cell interiors illustrate various dense molecular landscapes, which feature common cellular processes such as [[Neurotransmission|synaptic transmission]], [[Cytoskeleton|cytoskeletal]] remodeling, and [[Viral entry|viral uptake]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/this-painting-shows-what-might-look-like-when-zika-infects-cell-180959507/|title=This Painting Shows What It Might Look Like When Zika Infects a Cell|last=Fessenden|first=Marissa|date=2016-06-21|website=Smithsonian|access-date=2019-07-11}}</ref> Goodsell's artwork typically depicts a molecular snapshot of the inside of a cell, filled with highly simplified protein structures in a approachable style in order to capture overall organization of intracellular protein complexes without overwhelming detail.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/observations/turning-a-killer-virus-into-award-winning-art-video/|title=Turning a Killer Virus into Award-Winning Art [Video]|last=Augenbraun|first=Eliene|date=2016-03-22|website=Scientific American Blog|language=en}}</ref>

Goodsell's cell interiors are often displayed at an effective 1,000,000x magnification for consistency.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.asbmb.org/asbmbtoday/201108/features/Goodsell/|title=David Goodsell: The master of mol art|last=Shikov|first=Sergei|date=2011|website=www.asbmb.org|publisher=American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Today}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Goodsell|first=David|date=2016-02-26|title=Cellular Landscapes in Watercolor|journal=Journal of Biocommunication|language=en|volume=40|issue=1|pages=e6 |doi=10.5210/jbc.v40i1.6627|pmid=36407827 |pmc=9138463 |issn=0094-2499|doi-access=free}}</ref> The paintings therefore share a consistent style, aiming to make interpretation easy and as intuitive as possible.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Goodsell|first=David S.|date=2011|title=Eukaryotic cell panorama|journal=Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Education|language=en|volume=39|issue=2|pages=91–101|doi=10.1002/bmb.20494|pmid=21445900|s2cid=37998506|issn=1539-3429|doi-access=free}}</ref> Many of his illustrations are published in the "Molecule of the Month" series by the [[Protein Data Bank]] (PDB), an archive of [[protein structure]]s.<ref name=":1">{{cite web|url=http://www.exploratorium.edu/traits/goodsell.html|title=Interview with David Goodsell|last=Miller|first=Mary K.|website=exploratorium.edu|publisher=Exploratorium Magazine|accessdate=3 April 2015}}</ref>

== Illustration ==

=== Process ===
For individual proteins, Goodsell's illustrations are directly generated from solved [[Protein structure|protein structures]] deposited in the [[Protein Data Bank|PDB]] using custom computer renderings that he wrote in [[Fortran]] (now released as an online illustration tool).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ccsb.scripps.edu/illustrate/|title=Non-photorealistic Biomolecular Illustration|website=ccsb.scripps.edu|access-date=2019-07-20}}</ref> Representations of large [[Biomolecular complex|macromolecular complexes]] or [[Macromolecular crowding|crowded cellular environments]] require interpretation and synthesis of multiple different types of scientific imaging.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.abc.net.au/radionational/programs/sundayextra/finding-beauty-in-deadly-viruses/7580594|title=Finding beauty in deadly viruses|last=Calderwood|first=Kathleen|date=2016-07-08|website=ABC Radio National|access-date=2019-07-11}}</ref> These include X-ray crystallography and [[Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy of proteins|NMR]] for protein components, [[Cryo Electron Tomography|cryo electron tomography]] for larger complexes, and [[Super-resolution microscopy|super-res light microscopy]] and [[electron microscopy]] for the cellular environment.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.rutgers.edu/feature-focus/art-science/20110224|title=The Art of Science|last=Lally|first=Robin|date=2011-02-24|website=Rutgers Today|language=en}}</ref> In these cases, the focus is on portraying the relative scales, orientations and interactions between the components.<ref name=":3" />

=== Awards and recognition ===
In 2022, Goodsell was the recipient of the Carl Brändén Award.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Outreach and Education |url=https://cdn.rcsb.org/rcsb-pdb/general_information/news_publications/newsletters/2022q4/outreach.html |access-date=2024-01-08 |website=cdn.rcsb.org}}</ref> The award honors an outstanding protein scientist who has also made exceptional contributions in the areas of education and/or service.

== Bibliography ==
In addition to scientific papers, Goodsell is the author of several scientific books with a focus on illustration:<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.americanscientist.org/authors/detail/david-goodsell|title=Author: David Goodsell|date=2011-06-12|website=americanscientist.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110612225149/http://www.americanscientist.org/authors/detail/david-goodsell|archive-date=2011-06-12|url-status=|access-date=2019-07-11}}</ref>

*''Atomic Evidence: Seeing the Molecular Basis of Life'' (Springer International, 2016)
*''Bionanotechnology: Lessons from Nature'' (J. Wiley and Sons, 2004)
* ''Our Molecular Nature: The Body's Motors, Machines, and Messages'' (Springer-Verlag, 1996)

* ''The Machinery of Life'' (Springer-Verlag, 1993).
